5.text: The categorical assertion of Mr. Gondatti, however, that the Asiatic Eskimo

6.text: came from St. Lawrence Island, seems to me highly improbable, though I also

7.text: assume that the Asiatic Eskimo are not indigenous to the Pacific coast. Whether

8.text: they came from the Arctic coast of Asia or that of America is another question;

9.text: but, in any case, they migrated from north to south, and St. Lawrence Island

10.text: is the limit of their migrations. W. H. Dall repeats a statement of a native

11.text: of Plover Bay by the name of Nokum, who told that the “Bowhead [whale]

12.text: men” came to Asia long ago from the Islands to the northeast (the Diomedes),

13.text: and were allowed by the “Deer men” to settle on the barren, rocky coast.¹

14.text: The inhabitants of the Diomede Islands are called Yɪkɪrg̣aˊulɪt (“the [large]

15.text: mouthed”), from yɪkɪˊrg̣ɪn (“mouth”), the labrets which they wore in former

16.text: times having made their mouths their most conspicuous feature. The American

17.text: Continent is called Kɪˊɪmɪn.² Its inhabitants are called Kɪˊɪmɪlɪt, and also

19.text: It is a question open to discussion, whether in former times there were

20.text: any Eskimo villages on the Arctic coast. At present there are none except

21.text: Nɵˊɵkan; though some of the inhabitants of Uweˊlen, the nearest settlement

22.text: to the west, are Eskimo. The older travellers, such as Lütke and Wrangell,

23.text: mention a few tribal names supposed to be Eskimo, as Onkilon and Namollo;

24.text: but of these, the former resembles the Chukchee añqaˊlɪn,³ while Namollo brings

25.text: to mind the Koryak word for “maritime settlers,” nɪˊmɪḷu, which in Chukchee

26.text: takes the form nɪˊmɪlɪt (“inhabitants”), from nɪˊmnɪm (“habitation”).

27.text: Wrangell, and also Nordenskiöld, following in his footsteps,⁴ mention an

28.text: Eskimo tribe that some two hundred years ago occupied the whole Arctic

29.text: coast from Cape Shelagskoy (Erri) to Bering Strait, and was driven away by

30.text: the Chukchee. They base their chief argument upon the difference between

31.text: the actual Chukchee dwellings and the remnants of the old underground houses

32.text: found here and there. In reality, this difference means nothing more than

33.text: that, with the increase of reindeer-breeding, the underground houses, being

34.text: unwholesome, and requiring a great consumption of oil, were gradually abandoned

35.text: by both Eskimo and Chukchee for another type of house, probably also ancient,
